summary: Defines a new GSS-API function that lets an application store delegated credentials, and other credentials, in the implicit credential store. This allows applications to use delegated credentials just like any others they hold.

eli5.summary: If someone lends you a key card, you need somewhere to put it so doors recognize it. This gives programs a place to keep a borrowed key.

questions: how to store delegated credentials in gss-api
why do delegated credentials disappear after exec
what does overwrite_cred do in gss_store_cred
subtitle: A GSS-API function that saves delegated credentials into the normal credential store so ordinary calls can use them.

tldr.problem: The GSS-API has no way to put a delegated credential into the credential store, so an acceptor can only use it directly and loses it when a process is replaced with exec().
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5588 adds GSS_Store_cred(), which stores a given credential, or one mechanism element of it, in the current credential store, with options to overwrite an existing credential and to make it the default.
tldr.outcome: Delegated credentials can then be acquired like any other credential, for example by child processes of an acceptor. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Boolean arguments
facts.value: OM_uint32; 0 is FALSE, non-zero is TRUE

today: RFC 5588 is a Proposed Standard, published in July 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Delegated Credentials
sections.content:
The GSS-API (RFC 2743) assumes that credentials live in an implicit credential store. Applications get them out with GSS_Acquire_cred() and GSS_Add_cred(), or by using the default credential. Several stores may exist on one host, but only one can be reached by those calls at any given time.

A delegated credential is not in the acceptor's store, nor in the stores of the user contexts the acceptor may switch to. The GSS-API gives no way to make a delegated credential handle available to GSS_Acquire_cred(), and it has no credential import or export calls.

So an acceptor can only use a delegated handle directly, and only with GSS_Init_sec_context(), GSS_Inquire_cred*() and GSS_Release_cred(). The RFC calls this especially onerous on Unix, where a call to exec() replaces the process image and destroys any delegated credential handle held in the process.
sections.eli5: Imagine a borrowed key card that only works while you hold it in your hand. The moment you change rooms, it vanishes. That is the problem this solves.

sections.title: What GSS_Store_cred() Does
sections.content:
GSS_Store_cred() stores, in the current credential store, a credential that was either acquired from a different store or accepted as a delegated credential. The text says it makes delegated credentials generally as useful as credentials from GSS_Acquire_cred() and GSS_Add_cred().

A caller can store one mechanism element at a time by naming a mechanism OID. When the major status is not GSS_S_COMPLETE in that case, the minor status SHOULD carry a mechanism-specific value. Initiator usage, acceptor usage or both can be stored, as chosen by the cred_usage input.

On success, the outputs cred_usage_stored and mech_elements_stored tell the caller what was actually stored.
sections.eli5: It is like a coat check for borrowed keys. You hand the key over once, and later any door in the building can find it.

sections.title: Inputs and Outputs
sections.content:
The function takes five inputs:

  • input_cred_handle: the credential to store. It MUST NOT be GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL.
  • cred_usage: 0 for initiate-and-accept, 1 for initiate-only, 2 for accept-only.
  • desired_mech_element: if GSS_C_NULL_OID, all elements of the credential are stored; otherwise only the element for that mechanism.
  • overwrite_cred: if TRUE, replace any credential for the same principal in the store. Without it, existing credentials are not replaced.
  • default_cred: advisory. If TRUE, the stored credential SHOULD be made the default credential.

If the store has no default credential, the implementation MAY make the stored credential the default whatever default_cred says. The outputs are major_status, minor_status, mech_elements_stored and cred_usage_stored. The last one is useful when the input usage was initiate-and-accept.
sections.eli5: You tell the coat check which key, what it opens, whether to swap out an older key of yours, and whether it should be your main key.

sections.title: Return Codes
sections.content:
The function reports its result through these major status codes:

  • GSS_S_COMPLETE: the credentials were stored.
  • GSS_S_CREDENTIALS_EXPIRED: the input credentials had expired, or expired before they could be stored.
  • GSS_S_NO_CRED: no input credentials were given.
  • GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE: the credential store is not available.
  • GSS_S_DUPLICATE_ELEMENT: an element could not be stored because a credential for the same principal exists and overwrite_cred was FALSE.
  • GSS_S_FAILURE: the credential could not be stored for some other reason.
sections.eli5: The coat check answers with one of a few replies: done, your key is too old, you gave me nothing, the closet is closed, you already have a key here, or something else went wrong.

sections.title: C Bindings
sections.content: The C binding follows the style of the GSS-APIv2 C bindings (RFC 2744) and is named gss_store_cred. The two booleans, overwrite_cred and default_cred, are typed as OM_uint32: 0 means FALSE and any non-zero value means TRUE.
sections.eli5: For programmers using C, the function has a fixed shape, and yes or no answers are written as zero or not zero.

sections.title: Intended Use
sections.content: The intended use is to make delegated credentials available to child processes of GSS-API acceptor applications. In the RFC's pseudo-code, the acceptor finishes a GSS_Accept_sec_context() loop and gets an initiator name and a delegated credential handle. It then checks that the client is authorized for a requested username and changes the user context. On Unix-type platforms that may mean calling setuid(). Finally it calls gss_store_cred() with the delegated handle.
sections.eli5: A visitor lends a server a key. The server first checks the visitor is allowed in, then puts the key where the server's helpers can find it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Acceptor applications MUST only store delegated credentials into appropriate credential stores, and only after proper authorization of the authenticated initiator principal to the requested services.

Acceptors that have no use for delegated credentials MUST release them. Acceptors using the C bindings can simply pass a NULL value for the delegated_cred_handle argument to gss_accept_sec_context().
sections.eli5: Only keep a borrowed key after you have checked the visitor is allowed in, and hand back keys you do not need.

data.title: gss_store_cred
data.code:
OM_uint32 gss_store_cred(
   OM_uint32         *minor_status,
   gss_cred_id_t     input_cred_handle,
   gss_cred_usage_t  cred_usage,
   const gss_OID     desired_mech,
   OM_uint32         overwrite_cred,
   OM_uint32         default_cred,
   gss_OID_set       *elements_stored,
   gss_cred_usage_t  *cred_usage_stored)
